title: SYMBIOSIS BETWEEN BIOPHILIC DESIGN AND RESTORATIVE HEALING ENVIRONMENTS: THE IMPACT ON OVERALL WELL-BEING OF URBAN DWELLERS

stimuli.description: Three digital renderings of 'transitional spaces' (e.g., floor-to-ceiling glass curtain wall, clerestory windows, windows at eye level) to assess perceived 'exploration and discovery'.
Three digital renderings of 'natural lighting' applications (e.g., large glass curtain wall, windows at eye level, clerestory windows) to assess perceived 'reverence and spirituality'.
Three digital renderings of 'inside-outside spaces' (e.g., exterior trellis system) to assess perceived 'prospect and refuge'.
Three digital renderings of 'water features' (e.g., large cascading waterfall) to assess perceived 'change and metamorphosis'.
Three digital renderings of 'living greenery' (e.g., green living wall, planter box, potted trees) to assess perceived 'change and metamorphosis'.

limitations: Data collected was not modeled for other areas of nature-driven design such as sustainable design and/or environmental design.
Data analysis was fixed solely to gain the perception of specified biophilic elements in a restorative healing environment and excluded those elements not present in the developed framework.
Participants were shown only three digital renderings that depicted each biophilic attribute being studied; the digital renderings represented only one view of a larger, three-dimensional space.
Data collected was based on the perception of that particular digital rendering of the space, as participants were not able to physically experience and/or occupy each space that was being presented.
The building selected to model design ideas is located in a dense urban environment.
The conceptual and final design excluded biophilic attributes deemed unachievable based on the building’s size, geographic location, or physical adjacencies limited by its urban context.

The design focused on mimicking realistic limitations and opportunities that the interiors of a space in a highly dense urban environment would face when introducing selected attributes of biophilic design.
Generalization to other urban built environments was not warranted.
The study did not investigate the perception of biophilic design in any aspects other than those in the alternative healthcare and restorative settings.
Generalization to other types of healthcare environments was not warranted.
The framework only included nine of the 70+ biophilic design attributes defined by Stephen Kellert, allowing only those listed to be surveyed and emphasized.
Some may argue that based on personal perception, the chosen nine biophilic attributes may not be the most vital design attributes to emphasize.
